title: 水晶宫的恐龙：伦敦维多利亚时代的史前英国想象（Rory Walsh 现场踏查）
originalTitle: The Crystal Palace dinosaurs, London’s Victorian vision of prehistoric Britain
bodyText: Rory Walsh explores South London’s Victorian vision of prehistoric Britain Southeast London. August lately over, and a new Prime Minister sitting in Downing Street. Implacable summer weather. As little mud on the ground as if the waters had but wholly retired from the face of the earth, and it’s wonderful to meet a megalosaurus, ten metres long or so, gazing like an elephantine lizard on Sydenham Hill… Almost 175 years after Charles Dickens wrote the opening of Bleak House, a walk through Crystal Palace Park today invites the above reworking. Dickens imagined a megalosaurus crawling unnoticed through winter mud in his version. The one I’m looking at, a stern green giant with sharp teeth and hunched shoulders, stands proudly on display after Britain’s driest summer. The megalosauruses are among the biggest of the Crystal Palace Park dinosaurs. The 30 or so statues, built just after Bleak House was published, were the world’s first life-sized models of extinct animals. When they were unveiled to the public in 1855, the dinosaurs were a sensation. Besides visual spectacle, they were intended to educate Victorian visitors about the emerging science of palaeontology. The statues were placed in a carefully landscaped Geological Court. Winding footpaths still lead around three scenic islands set within a tidal lake. The islands represent scenes from the Palaeozoic, Mesozoic and Cenozoic eras, with the statues chronologically arranged to create a ‘walk through Deep Time’. Alongside them, a set of ‘Geological Illustrations’ showcases Britain’s geological and mineral resources. Massive amounts of quarried rock were transported to the park from across the country, including Yorkshire, the Peak District and the Dorset coast. A bridge overlooks a reproduction stratified cliff, complete with geological faults and a thick seam of coal. Elsewhere are artificial outcrops of chalk and sandstone. Initially, the site had a replica lead mine. The statues themselves were made in plaster from clay moulds. The larger ones are lined with enough material to build a house. An iguanodon, for example, contains 600 bricks, 900 tiles and more than 30 metres of iron framework. Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins, the noted sculptor who cast them, consulted the latest research to decide what creatures may have looked like. Exquisite details include the complex eyes of the ichthyosaurs and layered fur on the giant ground sloth.

title: 南苏丹戈罗姆安置营里的 LGBTQ+ 难民（作者田野访谈与自摄影像）
originalTitle: LGBTQ+ refugees face persecution in South Sudan’s Gorom settlement
bodyText: LGBTQ+ refugees have fled persecution across East Africa in search of safety. In South Sudan’s Gorom Refugee Settlement, many say that the violence and harassment have followed them By Kate Plummer When Amy arrived in South Sudan’s Gorom Refugee Settlement, she hoped she would finally be offered protection after three volatile years. The 31-year-old transgender woman had left Uganda in 2021, fearing persecution. She had questioned her sexual and gender identity from a young age but had grown up in a conservative religious family in a country with harsh anti-homosexuality laws. She felt muzzled. If you tell people about your sexuality, ‘your head is chopped off, anything can happen’, she said. Amy’s growing fear about her future in Uganda came to a head when, aged 18, her family caught her with her male netball coach, whom she had started dating in secret. Scared, she ran away, eventually reaching a refugee camp in Kenya before moving to Gorom when proposed anti-LGBTQ+ legislation threatened to upend her life again. But for Amy and other LGBTQ+ people in Gorom, refuge has brought little security. Life remains a daily struggle against discrimination, hate speech, verbal harassment, intimidation and targeted attacks because of their sexualities and gender identities. Gorom Refugee Settlement lies 26 kilometres southwest of Juba, South Sudan’s capital. The camp, built in 2010, is under the authority of the South Sudanese government through its Commission for Refugee Affairs and is supported by several organisations, including UNHCR, the UN’s refugee agency, the Red Cross and Peace Winds. It was originally intended to house 2,500 refugees fleeing conflict in Ethiopia, but it’s now overflowing. According to a UNHCR spokesperson, some 16,000 refugees live in the settlement and on 22 June this year, the camp stopped registering new arrivals. The spokesperson declined to say how many of the refugees are LGBTQ+, citing confidentiality. Amy estimated the number at around 600. Image: LG Graphics Amy is one of several LGBTQ+ refugees who told Geographical about being beaten at night, attacked at water collection points and harassed by other refugees because of their sexual and gender identities. Some of the refugees, whose names have been changed to protect their identities, also said their businesses had been burnt down and that neighbours had sent them letters demanding that they leave the camp.

title: 黄眼企鹅只剩 117 对繁殖 pair：奥塔哥半岛的现场监测与定置网争议
originalTitle: As yellow-eyed penguins disappear, conservationists focus on deaths in fishing nets
bodyText: OTAGO PENINSULA, Aotearoa New Zealand — Sandfly Bay was long a key nesting area for yellow-eyed penguins ( Megadyptes antipodes ), noisy, pink-footed birds that spend long days foraging at sea. But this wild beach on the Otago Peninsula, like others nearby, has gone quiet. In 2024, the last breeding-age female at Sandfly Bay, who’d been consistently producing chicks for a dozen years, drowned in a fishing net. Fishing has been one of many factors driving the species, which is only found in Aotearoa New Zealand, toward extinction. In the 2008-2009 breeding season, there were 739 breeding pairs in the “mainland” New Zealand population, which includes pairs on nearby islands. But the population has dropped since then to 117 pairs — a decline of more than 80%. These figures don’t account for yellow-eyed penguins on New Zealand’s remote southern islands, which are poorly surveyed. The IUCN, the global wildlife conservation authority, listed the species as endangered in its last assessment, in 2020, when the mainland population was still twice what it is now. Several experts told Mongabay that the species’ chances of survival are slim, though most said they still had faith. “I think I’d always like to say that there’s hope because otherwise why do you do what you do, but things are pretty dire,” Trudi Webster, a marine scientist who’s worked on research and conservation of the species for the past decade, told Mongabay. A number of organizations are working to save the yellow-eyed penguin, and much of the conservation concern has centered on set-net fishing. Set nets act as a vertical wall anchored in the water that catches fish by their gills or entangles them. They’ve drowned numerous yellow-eyed penguins. Over the objections of fishers, the New Zealand government recently opted to make a set-net closure around the Otago Peninsula permanent and set an annual fishing-related mortality limit of four penguins. Conservationists say it’s not enough. A yellow-eyed penguin lingers between the trees and the beach at a nesting site in Moeraki managed by Penguin Rescue. Image by Edward Carver for Mongabay. A treasured species, a multitude of threats Yellow-eyed penguins are an iconic species in New Zealand, appearing on the $5 bill and drawing tourists to Otago. Stuffed yellow-eyed penguins even greet travelers at the airport in Dunedin, the area’s main city.

title: 乡野日记：蝴蝶群与 861 年前的克罗根战役重演
originalTitle: Country diary: A tangle of butterflies and battle re-enactments | Paul Evans
bodyText: I ’m telling the story from a pub in the bailey opposite the ruins of Oswestry Castle. There in 1165, Henry II, the Angevin (Anglo-Norman) king of England, gathered troops from the Marcher Lords to advance on an alliance of Welsh princes for control of the Marches. The previous Sunday, 861 years later, we went the same way as Henry’s army to Chirk Castle , Castell Y Waun a’r Ardd, to see a re-enactment of the Battle of Crogen . The present castle wasn’t built back then and the battle at Crogen was in the Ceiriog Valley below. Henry had sent woodsmen to raze woodland in the valley to remove the Welsh advantage, but he left one oak, Quercus petraea , at which Owain Gwynedd gathered his army. That tree became the Pontfadog oak – a giant, the oldest British oak, and survived as the National Tree of Wales, much loved and storied until it blew down in a storm in 2013 at an estimated 1,600 years old. I have a small fragment of it given to me by the longtime Guardian environment editor John Vidal . A small copper butterfly. Photograph: Bob Eade/Butterfly Conservation/PA The battle re-enactment, with crashing swords and shields in the colours of Marcher lords and Welsh princes, fine horses and boinging arrows, was fun to watch with a running commentary giving a sense of what was happening and who was doing what. Histories vary about whether this was a great battle, isolated harassments or no fighting at all, but the outcome was the same: the Welsh won. The history of the Marches, like the traumatised, ghost-ridden ground itself, has been a contested space for centuries. It was fascinating to talk to people dedicated to making the past come to life for modern audiences. Over the castle garden wall, the past and present were weaving together in micro-dramas of moment. Two clouded yellow butterflies, Colias croceus , which had migrated here from north Africa or southern Europe, were flickering over herbaceous borders and lawns. Given the massive decline in insect populations, that pastoral scene had a spirit of resistance. And as if to demonstrate a mystical kind of heraldry and valour of a far more ancient territorial warrior, a small copper , Lycaena phlaeas , flourished his wings. Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com Explore more on these topics Butterflies Country diary Rural affairs Shropshire England Trees and forests Heritage Wildlife features Share Reuse this content

title: 解读：海平面上升为何是"人类、遗产与自然的生存威胁"
originalTitle: Explainer: How sea level rise poses an ‘existential threat’ to humans, heritage and nature
bodyText: For millions of people around the world, rising sea levels are already reshaping economies, livelihoods and cultures. The world’s oceans are currently rising at a faster rate than at any time in at least the past three millennia, with human influence the “ dominant cause ” of sea level rise since at least 1970. At the UN general assembly in New York this week, world leaders are set to adopt a high-level declaration on the “existential threats” posed by sea level rise. The declaration notes: “Sea level rise is not a distant scenario, but a real and lived experience for many.” On average, global sea levels rose by 20 centimetres (cm) between 1901 and 2018. This is due to both the melting of glaciers and ice sheets and the expansion of seawater as it warms, as well as changes in land-water storage . The rate of the rise has accelerated in recent years, with ocean levels rising 10.6cm since 1993. Sea level rise can vary locally due to seismic and volcanic activity, groundwater extraction and changes to the Earth’s surface resulting from ice melt. Under a moderate-emissions scenario , scientists predict that global average sea level will rise an additional 56cm by 2100, relative to a 1995-2014 baseline. Here, Carbon Brief unpacks some of the key ways that sea level rise threatens both societies and ecosystems. Cities and coastal communities Biodiversity and coastal ecosystems Small island developing states Coral reefs Heritage sites Cities and coastal communities Biodiversity and coastal ecosystems Small island developing states Coral reefs Heritage sites Cities and coastal communities Around 770 million people – 10% of the world’s population – are at “acute risk” of negative impacts from sea level rise, according to a report from the UN secretary general released last month. (The report defines locations at acute risk as those that are less than five metres above the high-tide line.) The people at risk include the residents of several of the world’s largest cities , including Mumbai and Kolkata in India and Shenzhen and Guangzhou in China. It also encompasses the entire populations of many island nations. (See: Small island developing states .) There are two ways to consider sea level rise. Global-average sea level rise is the amount the ocean surface has moved upwards, on average, relative to a baseline. Relative, or local, sea level rise, is how much the ocean has risen in a given place.

title: 分析：卢拉任内至少保住 2 万平方公里亚马逊雨林
originalTitle: Analysis: Lula presidency saved at least 20,000km2 of Brazilian Amazon since 2022
bodyText: An area of Amazon forest roughly the size of the US state of New Jersey has remained standing due to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s leadership of Brazil, according to Carbon Brief analysis. Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election to become president of the nation that is home to nearly 60% of the Amazon rainforest. Forest loss surged during Bolsonaro’s far-right presidency and dropped sharply under the left-wing Lula, with Amazon deforestation likely to hit its lowest level on record this year. Now, as another presidential election approaches, Lula is facing off against Bolsonaro’s son, Flávio Bolsonaro, whose “ anti-environmental ” policies are similar to his father’s. Carbon Brief’s analysis suggests that at least 20,000 square kilometres (km2) of deforestation has been avoided since Lula took office and prioritised Amazon protection. The analysis is based on modelling by an international research team of an alternative scenario in which Brazil’s flagship forest code legislation was not enforced – a proxy for Jair Bolsonaro’s leadership. Experts tell Carbon Brief that this estimate is likely “conservative” and that actual deforestation under Bolsonaro could have been “much higher”. With Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro tied in the polls, the upcoming election is expected to significantly shape the level of environmental action in the world’s fourth-largest emitter, whose emissions are largely driven by deforestation. ‘Brazil is back’ When Jair Bolsonaro was president of Brazil between 2019 and 2022, he championed the nation’s powerful agribusiness sector and oversaw an unprecedented increase in Amazon deforestation. Bolsonaro weakened regulations, slashed federal agency budgets and empowered illegal activities in the Amazon, while attacking Indigenous and environmental groups. This meant that the forest code – Brazil’s flagship legislation that requires landowners to preserve and restore forest on their property – was not properly enforced. After Lula’s presidential victory in 2022, he promised to target “ zero deforestation ” by 2030, telling the COP27 UN climate summit that “Brazil is back”. Lula rolled back Bolsonaro’s wave of deregulation and reinstated a deforestation “ action plan ”. Led by celebrated environmentalist Marina Silva, the environment ministry scaled up enforcement and policing activities in the Amazon. As a result, annual deforestation in the Amazon has more than halved from 11,594km2 per year in 2022 to 5,731km2 in 2025.

title: 分析：尼泊尔申请的 2000 万美元"损失与损害"仅覆盖洪灾成本的 0.7%
originalTitle: Analysis: Nepal’s $20m ‘loss-and-damage’ claim only covers 0.7% of flood costs
bodyText: The Nepali government has requested $20m from the UN fund for “ loss and damage ”, following the devastating floods that hit the country in late August. This amounts to just 0.7% of the $2.7bn it has estimated in “physical damage” to infrastructure and “economic losses” from the flooding, according to Carbon Brief analysis. The $20m request would, nevertheless, make Nepal the fourth-largest claimant to the UN loss-and-damage fund, which is intended to help deal with climate-related disasters. Developing countries have already made 176 applications to the UN fund for responding to loss and damage , requesting, in total, $2.8bn to help recover from a variety of damaging events, such as drought, floods and storms. Yet, to date, predominantly developed nations have only pledged $0.8bn to support the fund. This means requests to the fund are already three times larger than the total amount pledged, raising questions about its potential to respond to emergencies. As yet, no funding has been paid out of the fund to developing countries grappling with intensifying and more frequent climate change-induced disasters since it was established in 2023. Nepal’s needs On 26 August, Nepal was hit by flash floods following a catastrophic rock-ice avalanche in the Himalayan border region. The flooding has killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing . Days later, the Nepali government sought an “urgent response” from the board of the UN fund for climate-driven loss and damage. It subsequently requested $20m in “ financial compensation ” from the fund. This is the maximum amount that can currently be requested for a single project. “ Loss and damage ” is a term used to describe how climate change is causing serious and, in many cases, irreversible impacts around the world. Nations established the UN fund in 2023, after decades of effort by climate-vulnerable nations. Nepal’s national disaster management authority has now released an extensive rapid preliminary assessment of “damage and needs” from the floods. As the chart below shows, Nepal’s $20m loss-and-damage claim would only cover 0.7% of what authorities describe as $2.7bn in “total damage and loss” from the floods. When accounting for another $4.8bn in “recovery and reconstruction” costs – part of how loss and damage is internationally defined – then Nepal’s $20m claim would be just 0.3% of the needs it estimates.

title: 热成像揭示极端高温的"隐形不公正"：欧洲今夏至少 3 万人死亡
originalTitle: Revealing the Invisible Injustice of Extreme Heat
bodyText: The extreme heat scientists have warned about for decades came to Europe again this summer, killing at least 30,000 people like a silent, invisible plague. It came for poor people, the very young and very old, and those suffering from debilitating conditions. The final toll will likely be higher. A 2024 United Nations report estimated about 175,000 annual heat-related deaths across Europe, and total deaths in European Union countries spiked above 60,000 in 2022 and 2024. The heat started earlier than ever, in late May, and kept coming in deadly, unrelenting waves that destroyed crops and vineyards, buckled railroad tracks, turned forests to kindling and dried up rivers and lakes. When it settled heavily over Bologna, Italy , in late June, residents of the industrial region said it was like a stifling, life-threatening force that you feel in your bones, transforming streets and buildings into radiators blasting warmth day and night, making routine outdoor chores dangerous. Heat is hard to see, but you feel it in the pavement, in the walls of poorly insulated apartments, in sweat that never quite dries and a bedroom that just won’t cool down. And people do not experience it equally. Bologna photographer Michele Lapini made those differences visible, using his iPhone and a thermal sensor to document temperatures in homes, workplaces and public spaces as the heat gripped the city. The images show that construction workers in direct sun, delivery riders crossing the city and residents of old apartment buildings and poorly cooled senior centers inhabit radically different thermal worlds than people with access to air conditioning, shade and well-insulated homes. Piazza Maggiore was between 93 and 103 degrees Fahrenheit at 9:28 p.m. during the “Il Cinema Ritrovato” festival, promoted by the Cineteca di Bologna. Federico, 56, works as a meteorologist; a few years ago, he invested his savings to improve his apartment’s energy efficiency using renewable energy, keeping the temperature around 70 degrees Fahrenheit at 5:48 p.m. Michele, 31, works as a metalworker and lives in a rented apartment on the same floor as Federico’s, but without any energy efficiency upgrades or air conditioning. His apartment was above 90 degrees Fahrenheit at 5:57 p.m. Lapini said he felt a great sense of resignation as he talked with people about the heat. What could they do? They had no choice but to work. They couldn’t move or get a permit to install air conditioning, or afford it.

title: 访谈：强到"没有学名"的厄尔尼诺——NOAA 新指标意味着什么
originalTitle: Incoming El Niño Is so Extreme It Doesn’t Have a Scientific Name
bodyText: Daniel Swain has made a name for himself studying the extremes of a warming planet. Fires, floods, droughts, heat, storms: if it’s a record breaker, Swain has probably studied it. As a weather and climate research scientist at UCLA’s Institute of the Environment and Sustainability , Swain has dedicated his life to understanding so-called “outlier events” and how climate change is super-charging them. Then, he explains them, and not just to fellow scientists. He devotes over 1,000 hours a year to climate communication for the public. Swain is the mind behind “Weather West,” and coined the term “Ridiculously Resilient Ridge ” in December 2013, as a first year graduate student, for the high pressure ridge perpetuating the 2011-2017 northern California and Pacific Northwest drought. As a climate scientist, and life long Californian, he has been keeping a close eye on the current El Niño. Based on a recent study in Science , the current El Niño is likely the strongest in over a millennium. Following this revelation, the U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres warned, "The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up." Officials from Britain to Los Angeles are issuing advisories for residents to prepare and stock up on essentials in preparation for this historic El Niño. In a recent interview, Swain and Inside Climate News reporter Nina Dietz discussed why this El Niño is unlike anything we’ve seen before, and what it could mean for California and beyond: DANIEL SWAIN: So El Niño is a recharge oscillator, which is effectively a battery. The tropical oceans are a big heat sink. The tropics are warm, there's a lot of sun directly on the water, and then the currents subduct some of that heat to deeper layers. But then, you reach a point where there's so much energy in the Pacific that it becomes unstable, and the system needs to equilibrate. The way it does that is through an El Niño. Climate scientist Daniel Swain. Credit: Courtesy of Daniel Swain This is why El Niño and La Niña, the El Niño Southern Oscillation or ENSO collectively, is semi-cyclical, coming around every two-seven years or so. That's something you can take to the bank. We can view it as a battery, because there is a certain point beyond which it's not going to continue to overcharge. So El Niño is the ocean system discharging a full battery. We're going into extreme territory with this one, probably record breaking.

title: 马里布百年的"沙债"到期：冲刷点消失与海岸沉积物预算
originalTitle: A Century of Sand Debt Comes Due in Malibu
bodyText: On a clean summer swell, the wave at Malibu’s Surfrider Beach arrives from the south, wraps around a cobblestone point and unspools toward the pier in a long, shimmering wave that can carry a surfer for hundreds of feet. It breaks slowly, forgivingly, over rounded stones that were delivered by Malibu Creek across millennia. The beach plays an outsized role in American and surf culture, inspiring the films “Gidget” and “The Endless Summer” and the songs of the Beach Boys. The point produced the longboarding style that still bears the place’s name: In Australia, longboards are called “Malibus.” Kassia Meador has been reading this wave for nearly 30 years. She was 15 the summer she first paddled out at Surfrider Beach, and she has spent the decades since becoming one of the most recognizable longboarders in the world. She calls it, without hesitation, the best wave on the planet. Lately, when Meador paddles out, something is missing beneath her: the beach. The sand at Surfrider Beach has thinned to the point where, at high tide, the ocean reaches almost to the Pacific Coast Highway. The wave itself has changed shape; the three distinct points that made Malibu’s Surfrider Beach have collapsed into one, she said. “It bunches everybody together,” she said. There’s more crowding and more tension in the water, and less of the wave that made the place worth protecting. What’s happening at Malibu is about human intervention—a century of dams, seawalls and paved-over rivers that have starved this coastline of the sediment that builds its beaches. But it is becoming a climate story, fast, because a coast stripped of its natural defenses is a coast with nothing left to absorb what’s coming. And what’s coming this winter is a lot. NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center has an El Niño Advisory in effect and puts the odds of a very strong event this fall and winter at greater than 90 percent —it recently broke the highest surface temperature recorded for this phenomenon, months before the projected peak. California Governor Gavin Newsom declared a statewide emergency on Monday in anticipation of heavy rainfall, high waves and flooding the phenomenon could bring. Malibu’s First Point is one of 57 surf breaks a team of scientists, working with the conservation group Save the Waves, assessed in a study published this year in the journal Climatic Change.

title: 调查：关键矿产战略盯上美国"被遗忘的野生动物走廊"（McDermitt 火山口实地）
originalTitle: The Trump Administration’s Critical Minerals Agenda Comes for America’s ‘Forgotten Wildlife Corridor’
bodyText: MCDERMITT CALDERA, Ore.—On a cold and overcast spring morning, Katie Fite stood in one of the country’s last sage-grouse strongholds, contemplating the wooden stakes in the ground that she fears warn of its destruction. Every spring, males of the chunky bird species with spiky tail feathers come to a dwindling number of locations to strut, pop their inflatable white neck pouches and make a “ paloop, paloop ” sound in an attempt to court a mate. As their name suggests, sage-grouse need sagebrush, the green-brown shrub that once dominated arid Western landscapes. But both the bird and its habitat are rapidly disappearing due to climate change, invasive species, wildfires and energy development. Now a mining company wants to extract lithium here. A greater sage-grouse flies through the Warner Mountains of Oregon. Credit: John Carlson/USFWS Millions of sage-grouse once filled the West, but federal data shows their numbers have plummeted 80 percent since 1965 as more than a million acres of the sagebrush landscape they depend on is lost every year. They’ve long teetered toward the endangered-species list . “We want to save sage-grouse?” Fite, public lands director for WildLands Defense, asked as she walked through the mating area, known as a lek, on the public lands where the McDermitt Lithium project would dig. “This is not how we do it. This is a travesty.” The project’s owner agreed to avoid drilling during the sage-grouse breeding season in an effort to avoid impacting a species that is easily put off mating if conditions aren’t just right. But there is so little sagebrush habitat left in the country, Fite said, that “you can’t even pretend to mitigate this.” Today, the U.S. has only one operating lithium mine—Albemarle’s Silver Peak in Nevada. By 2030, at least six new mining projects are predicted to be extracting lithium from American soil and another 13 will soon follow, according to a database compiled by Columbia Journalism Investigations and Inside Climate News. Scores more are proposed, their wooden stakes marking companies’ claims. This element of the energy transition—lithium is used in batteries for electric vehicles and energy storage—poses stark dilemmas in the communities atop the so-called white gold. Mining it uses and displaces water, and much of it is found in water-scarce regions. Tribal nations repeatedly harmed by past extraction are disproportionately located on or near lithium-rich lands. And then there’s vulnerable wildlife.

title: 评论：打击环境犯罪，要沿整条供应链追踪利润
originalTitle: To tackle environmental crime, track profits through the whole supply chain (commentary)
bodyText: The world has spent a decade trying to put a price on nature, yet the criminal economy has been putting a price on it for much longer. Land grabbing, illegal logging, illicit gold mining and wildlife trafficking are extremely lucrative and have become a serious drag on both sustainable development and climate action, a new op-ed argues, and its drivers must be addressed from where extraction begins all the way to corporate offices. “The world is still working out how much a standing forest is worth. Criminal markets settled on a price for a felled one long ago,” the authors write. This article is a commentary. The views expressed are those of the authors, not necessarily of Mongabay. The world has spent a decade trying to put a price on nature. Forests have become carbon sinks, while wetlands are increasingly described as natural infrastructure. Biodiversity is also being drawn into financial markets. Governments and investors have poured billions into carbon markets and conservation finance, including green bonds. Around them, a financial system is emerging on the assumption that intact ecosystems can generate enough economic value to protect them. A more destructive economy has been putting a price on nature for much longer. It makes money by extracting and selling it. Land grabbing, illegal logging, illicit gold mining and wildlife trafficking are usually treated as environmental offenses, so responsibility falls to park rangers, customs officials and specialized police. That view badly underestimates what is happening. In a new paper for the Brookings Institution, we argue that environmental crimes are a serious drag on both sustainable development and climate action. They damage ecosystems and weaken the institutions charged with governing them. They also drain revenue from legitimate companies and public coffers. Enforcement alone will not solve a problem that runs through trade, finance and local political economies. An IBAMA agent participates in a raid on an illegal logging and mining operation within an Indigenous reserve. Image courtesy of IBAMA. Global criminal economy No one knows exactly how large this economy has become. A widely cited estimate puts annual proceeds at between $110 billion and $281 billion, but the true figure is probably far higher, perhaps in the trillions. What makes the business so difficult to see is that much of the money disappears into transactions that look perfectly ordinary.

title: 卫报社论：超级厄尔尼诺——自然现象与人为愚蠢的致命组合
originalTitle: The Guardian view on a supersized El Niño: a natural phenomenon and human folly are a lethal combination | Editorial
bodyText: warnings are so grave that it is almost impossible to fully comprehend them. The descriptions of a super-sized, “Godzilla-level” El Niño already heating our planet would sound hyperbolic were they not issuing from eminent scientists. They say that the weather pattern, which occurs roughly every two to seven years, may be the strongest in at least a millennium. With its peak yet to come, the temperature rise in the Pacific Ocean has already surpassed the previous high. The consequence will be huge amounts of heat in an atmosphere already experiencing frighteningly higher temperatures due to the human-caused climate crisis. Next year is almost certain to be the hottest on record globally, breaking this year’s record. The World Food Programme has warned that 50 million people are likely to be pushed into acute hunger . Others estimate that the extra heat from El Niño alone will cause the deaths of 450,000 people by February , from Nigeria and Indonesia to the US. That extraordinary toll is in addition to those killed by the wildfires, droughts and floods it is likely to bring – and also to deaths caused by global heating. While the weather system develops in the Pacific Ocean, its knock-on effects will be felt far away. It increases drought risk in a large swathe of the world, while increasing rainfall elsewhere. India has already experienced a 50% shortfall in essential monsoon rains this month, affecting crops. In Sri Lanka, reservoirs for drinking water are running dry. European countries may be indirectly affected, with a stormier autumn, but the primary impact for them is likely to be on food supplies . Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary. Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty While there is ongoing debate about the impact of global heating on the pattern itself , a major study published last month found that strong El Niños in recent decades have been supercharged by the overheating of the planet due to fossil fuels. It is beyond doubt that the effects of this natural phenomenon are compounded by human-made folly and injustice. Domestically and internationally, the poorest will be worst hit, due to factors such as living conditions and underlying health, while being the least able to pay their way out of trouble. At the same time, the wealthy few will continue to enrich themselves from an economic system built on pumping out more emissions. Defenders of the status quo will continue to insist that we cannot afford to clean up our act.

title: 公开信：到 2030 年 everywhere 都要有太阳能
originalTitle: Our message to global leaders: we need solar power everywhere by the decade’s end | Open letter
bodyText: We the undersigned write this letter out of great fear and great hope. Over the last few months, we’ve seen the world set ablaze by both war and warming. From the conflict in Iran, which has claimed thousands of lives and disrupted billions more, to the series of ever worsening climate disasters, from wildfires in Europe to collapsing glaciers in Nepal, the world seems to be falling apart exactly when it needs to be coming together. We know that these crises are connected. The oil that governments fight over is also the carbon pollution that is warming our climate. The bad air quality in Delhi, the high price of fuel in Vietnam, the cost of electricity in the United States, the terrifying floods in the Himalayas – they all connect back to fossil fuels. Until we end that dependence, we’ll never be able to address the climate emergency and stop fighting these endless oil-soaked wars. That’s why today we are inviting the world to unite around a common cause: repowering the world with cheap, clean energy. We are calling on governments, businesses, institutions and the public to work together to provide clean, affordable energy to everyone, everywhere by 2030. From the nearly 1 billion people who still lack access to reliable electricity, to the billions more of us who pay too much for dirty fossil fuels. We know this world is within reach. Building clean energy is now the cheapest and fastest way to slash energy bills, reduce pollution, and provide electricity access to the places that need it most. With cheap solar, wind and batteries, we can create huge and rapid change. California is already using just half as much natural gas to generate electricity as it did three years ago, thanks to solar and batteries. In Pakistan, people have put up millions of solar panels in just months, relying on social media for instruction. Each month, millions more people across sub-Saharan Africa are getting electricity for the first time with home solar kits. This energy transition is already moving quickly – but we need it to go much quicker. And so we come together to urge two steps. First, we must build clean power for everyone. For the first time ever, we can reliably bring electricity to the one in 10 people on earth living without regular access. We ask everyone who can afford it to donate something so that others can turn the lights on for studying, cooking and medical care – and never have to think about a gallon of diesel or gas again.
